title: Projectile from a height (cliff)
what_it_asks: A particle is launched from a point above the ground, such as a cliff top, and lands at a known horizontal distance or after a known time. You find a time, a height, a speed or a greatest height. The idea is to treat the horizontal and vertical motions separately, with vertical displacement signed so that landing below the start is negative.
typical_structure: There are usually two to four parts, and there is always a diagram. A short opening part, often worth one mark, asks you to state a value or component. The later parts are longer, worth around three to six marks, and find a time, a height or a speed. A later part often builds on an earlier result. One question may include a show-that part, and another may ask how a refined model would change an answer.
mark_pattern: Short parts are often a single B1 for a stated value or component. Longer parts are mostly method marks followed by accuracy marks, such as M1 A1 A1ft or M1 A1 A1 M1. The opening M1 is for a vertical or horizontal equation of motion with sensible signs. The A1 after it rewards the correct result from that equation, usually a time. An A1ft lets you carry your own time or component into a later calculation, such as a speed. A sequence like M1 A1 M1 A1 M1 A1* ends in a show-that line, so the last mark needs a valid route to the printed result. Sometimes a part is marked M2 A2 M1, where the double-weighted method and accuracy marks come before a final method mark for using that result.

where_marks_leak.text: You set the whole velocity to zero at the top, rather than only the vertical component. The M1 for the greatest-height condition is lost, and the A1 after it goes too.
You give the final answer to the wrong number of decimal places or significant figures. The final A1 is lost even though the method was sound.
You quote an answer to more significant figures than the value of $g$ you used supports. The final A1 can be lost for this, so round to the accuracy the data justifies.
You factorise the quadratic in $t$ with the wrong signs and get a root of the wrong sign. The method mark for solving fails, and the A1 for the time, and any later dependent mark, goes with it.
A numerical slip in a correct method loses the A1 at that step. Later marks may survive only as A1ft if you use your own value correctly.

write_to_earn: Write the vertical equation of motion in symbols, such as $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, before you substitute anything.
Say where your origin is and which direction is positive, so a landing point below the start gets a negative displacement.
Put the two components $U\cos\alpha$ and $U\sin\alpha$ on their own line, because a stated component can earn a B1 by itself.
For the greatest height, write that the vertical speed is zero there, then use that in your equation.
In a show-that part, write the line just before the printed result, then the result itself, so the final starred mark is secure.
check_before_you_leave: Accuracy fits the value of g
